examTakeaway: Hypoxia constricts pulmonary arterioles, so blood is sent away from an unventilated region.
scenario: A 40-year-old man aspirates and the right lower lobe is collapsed. Blood gases show a smaller shunt than a complete loss of that lobe's vessels would suggest. He is on room air. A physiologist notes that flow to the collapsed lobe has fallen. He asks what the arterioles in that lobe did.
question: What did the arterioles in the unventilated lobe do?
explanation: Hypoxia constricts pulmonary arterioles, so blood is sent away from an unventilated region. They constricted, which is hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. They dilated would send more blood through unventilated lung and worsen the shunt. They ruptured is infarction, not a rapid flow shift. They became systemic bronchial arteries is not an acute change. They stopped responding to oxygen is the failure of this reflex, which is not what reduced the flow.

examTakeaway: A right shift of the oxygen curve unloads oxygen in working muscle, driven by heat, acid, and 2,3-BPG.
scenario: A 25-year-old runner has a muscle pH of 7.1 and a local temperature of 39 C during a sprint. Venous oxygen content from that leg is lower than at rest. Lung oxygen uptake is normal. He asks why the same hemoglobin let go of more oxygen in the muscle.
question: Which way did the dissociation curve move in that muscle?
options: No shift, only more blood flow
explanation: A right shift of the oxygen curve unloads oxygen in working muscle, driven by heat, acid, and 2,3-BPG. Right, unloading oxygen matches the acid and the heat. Left, holding oxygen tighter is what fetal hemoglobin and alkalosis do. No shift, only more blood flow, ignores the pH and temperature. Left, because of heat is the wrong direction for heat. Right, because of alkalosis is the wrong pH; he is acidotic.

examTakeaway: Fetal hemoglobin binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so its curve sits left and it can pull oxygen off maternal blood.
scenario: A 30-week fetus, the patient, has a lower PO2 than the mother, yet fetal blood leaving the placenta is well saturated. The mother's hemoglobin is adult type. The obstetrician asks which property lets fetal hemoglobin load oxygen at that lower PO2.
question: Which property lets fetal hemoglobin load at a lower PO2?
options: It binds 2,3-BPG tightly and the curve sits right
It unloads more easily than adult hemoglobin
It binds 2,3-BPG poorly and the curve sits left
correctAnswer: It binds 2,3-BPG poorly and the curve sits left
explanation: Fetal hemoglobin binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so its curve sits left and it can pull oxygen off maternal blood. It binds 2,3-BPG poorly and the curve sits left is that property. It binds 2,3-BPG tightly and the curve sits right would unload oxygen and lose the placental advantage. It cannot carry oxygen is false. It unloads more easily than adult hemoglobin is the right-shift behavior. It lacks heme would not carry oxygen at all.

examTakeaway: Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole, so blocking it drops filtration pressure when the afferent flow is already low.
scenario: A 70-year-old man with bilateral renal artery stenosis starts lisinopril. Creatinine rises from 1.2 to 2.4 mg/dL in a week. Blood pressure falls from 170/90 to 130/70 mm Hg. He asks why filtration fell when the pressure was still adequate for a normal kidney.
question: Which arteriole stopped holding filtration pressure up?
options: The afferent arteriole, which angiotensin constricts most
explanation: Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole, so blocking it drops filtration pressure when the afferent flow is already low. The efferent arteriole is the one angiotensin was constricting to keep glomerular pressure up behind the stenoses. The afferent arteriole, which angiotensin constricts most, is the wrong emphasis; the critical constriction for filtration pressure is efferent. The ureter is not a pressure arteriole. The vasa recta only serves the medulla. A glomerular vein is not the angiotensin target.

examTakeaway: The macula densa senses high salt delivery and constricts the afferent arteriole, which is tubuloglomerular feedback.
scenario: A 40-year-old man is given a drug that blocks proximal sodium reabsorption. More salt reaches the early distal tubule. Single-nephron filtration then falls. Blood pressure is unchanged. He asks what sensor saw the extra salt and what it did.
question: What did the macula densa do?
options: Released renin because salt delivery was high
explanation: The macula densa senses high salt delivery and constricts the afferent arteriole, which is tubuloglomerular feedback. Constricted the afferent arteriole is the response that lowered filtration. Dilated the afferent arteriole would raise filtration. Released renin because salt delivery was high is backward; high salt delivery suppresses renin. Inserted aquaporins is ADH. Secreted potassium is a collecting-duct job.

examTakeaway: Erythropoietin is made by peritubular fibroblasts when oxygen delivery falls, which is why a failing kidney causes anemia.
scenario: A 60-year-old man with a GFR of 15 mL/min has a hemoglobin of 9 g/dL. The smear is normocytic. Iron studies are normal. He has no blood loss. EPO level is low for the degree of anemia. He asks which kidney cell stopped making the hormone.
question: Which cell normally releases erythropoietin?
explanation: Erythropoietin is made by peritubular fibroblasts when oxygen delivery falls, which is why a failing kidney causes anemia. Peritubular fibroblast is the source, and his low EPO fits the low GFR. Podocyte injury causes protein leak, not this anemia. Macula densa senses salt. Mesangial cell supports the capillary. Proximal tubule brush border reabsorbs solutes and is not the EPO source.

examTakeaway: Surfactant lowers surface tension more in small alveoli, which is why they do not collapse into large ones.
scenario: A 29-week newborn grunts. The physiologist explains that without surfactant a small alveolus has higher collapsing pressure than a large one, by the law of Laplace. A dose of surfactant is given and the work of breathing falls. Temperature is 36.8 C.
question: Why does surfactant keep small alveoli open?
options: It lowers surface tension more as the radius shrinks
It raises surface tension in small alveoli
correctAnswer: It lowers surface tension more as the radius shrinks
explanation: Surfactant lowers surface tension more in small alveoli, which is why they do not collapse into large ones. It lowers surface tension more as the radius shrinks, offsetting Laplace. It raises surface tension in small alveoli would worsen collapse. It thickens the alveolar wall would impair gas exchange. It constricts bronchioles is not surfactant. It increases pulmonary artery pressure is hypoxic vasoconstriction, not surfactant.

examTakeaway: Most carbon dioxide travels as bicarbonate, and the chloride shift lets the red cell take up the chloride that bicarbonate leaves behind.
scenario: A 30-year-old man exercises. Venous PCO2 rises. In the red cell, CO2 becomes bicarbonate, which leaves the cell. The red-cell chloride rises at the same time. He asks why chloride entered the cell.
question: Why did chloride enter the red cell?
options: To bind hemoglobin as the main CO2 form
explanation: Most carbon dioxide travels as bicarbonate, and the chloride shift lets the red cell take up the chloride that bicarbonate leaves behind. To balance bicarbonate leaving is the chloride shift. To bind hemoglobin as the main CO2 form understates bicarbonate, which carries most of the CO2. To fuel the sodium pump is not why chloride rose with PCO2. To make surfactant happens in the lung, not this venous red cell. To shift the curve left is the opposite of the acid and CO2 effect.

examTakeaway: In the upright lung, the apex is dead-space-like because alveolar pressure exceeds blood flow, which is zone 1.
scenario: A 22-year-old man is upright and hypovolemic after a bleed. Blood pressure is 85/50 mm Hg. The apex of the lung is ventilated but almost unperfused. The base is still perfused. He asks which zone the apex has become.
question: Which zone is the unperfused apex?
explanation: In the upright lung, the apex is dead-space-like because alveolar pressure exceeds blood flow, which is zone 1. Zone 1 is ventilation without perfusion, worsened by low pulmonary artery pressure. Zone 3 is the base, where flow exceeds alveolar pressure. Zone 2 only at the base misplaces zone 2. A shunt zone is perfusion without ventilation, the opposite problem. A west zone 3 with edema is dependent flooding, not an empty apex.

examTakeaway: ANP is released by atrial stretch and dumps sodium, opposing the renin-aldosterone response to volume overload.
scenario: A 70-year-old man with heart failure has distended neck veins and a BNP of 2,000 pg/mL. He is volume overloaded. Urine sodium is higher than it was when he was dry. He asks which chamber stretch released the peptide that is wasting sodium.
question: Which stretch released the sodium-wasting peptide?
explanation: ANP is released by atrial stretch and dumps sodium, opposing the renin-aldosterone response to volume overload. Atrial and ventricular wall stretch releases ANP and BNP, which is why his urine sodium rose. Macula densa stretch is salt sensing, not this peptide. Carotid baroreceptor stretch alone changes sympathetic tone. A lung J-receptor senses interstitial pressure and causes rapid shallow breathing. The juxtaglomerular cell releases renin, which saves sodium.

examTakeaway: Intercalated cells secrete acid and reclaim bicarbonate, so damaging them causes a normal-gap acidosis with an inability to acidify the urine.
scenario: A 28-year-old woman has a bicarbonate of 16 mEq/L, a normal anion gap, and a urine pH of 6.8 despite the acidosis. Potassium is 3.0 mEq/L. She has kidney stones. Diarrhea is absent. She asks which cell failed to push acid into the urine.
question: Which cell failed?
explanation: Intercalated cells secrete acid and reclaim bicarbonate, so damaging them causes a normal-gap acidosis with an inability to acidify the urine. Alpha-intercalated cell is the acid secretor, and a urine pH of 6.8 during acidosis means it failed. Principal cell only handles sodium and potassium under aldosterone and ADH. Macula densa senses salt. Podocyte injury leaks protein. Mesangial cell supports the capillary, not distal acidification.
